Primary Data Domain: Asset prices, rates, randomness, events, cross-chain messages
On-Chain Footprint: Extensive Ethereum mainnet deployment; deeply integrated across L1s and L2s
Data Source Model: Aggregated data from multiple off-chain sources via independent node operators
Verification Mechanism: Cryptoeconomic aggregation, reputation, and staking-based security (staking expanding)
Who Can Submit Data: Permissioned professional node operators selected per feed
Who Can Challenge Data: Implicit via aggregation; explicit dispute via governance and fallback mechanisms
Freshness Guarantees: Feed-specific heartbeat intervals and deviation thresholds
Correctness Guarantees: Multi-source aggregation, medianization, and economic incentives
Failure Handling / Dispute Resolution: Automatic feed updates, circuit breakers, and fallback mechanisms
Security Model: Staking, slashing (rolling out), reputation, economic incentives
Cost Model: Per-feed update costs paid by consuming protocols
Value at Risk Alignment: High (feeds often secure billions in TVL)
Typical Protocol Dependencies: Lending protocols, DEXs, perps, stablecoins, RWAs, bridges
Downstream Economic Impact if Incorrect: Catastrophic—can trigger bad liquidations, insolvency, or broken pegs
Centralization Risk: Medium (node set curated; improving decentralization over time)
Known Exploits or Incidents: No major systemic price-feed exploit on Ethereum; isolated incidents in early ecosystem history
Description: Decentralized oracle network providing authoritative off-chain and cross-chain data to Ethereum smart contracts via independent node operators
Reason for Inclusion: Primary provider of authoritative oracle data for Ethereum; incorrect data would directly break protocol economics
Practitioner’s Note: Chainlink is often treated as default truth—practitioners must understand feed composition, update cadence, and fallback logic
Practitioner Validation Check: Verify which specific feeds are used, node count per feed, update thresholds, and fallback behavior under stress
Typical Users: DeFi protocols, derivatives platforms, stablecoins, bridges, RWAs

Primary Data Domain: Real-time asset prices (crypto, equities, FX, commodities)
On-Chain Footprint: Deployed on Ethereum mainnet and major L2s via pull-based oracle contracts
Data Source Model: First-party data from market makers, exchanges, and trading firms
Verification Mechanism: Publisher-signed data, aggregation, confidence intervals, and on-chain verification
Who Can Challenge Data: Implicit via aggregation; governance-driven changes to publishers
Correctness Guarantees: First-party sources + statistical aggregation with confidence bands
Availability Guarantees: High—off-chain data always available; on-chain availability on demand
Failure Handling / Dispute Resolution: Consumers pull latest price; fallback to last valid price if unavailable
Security Model: Reputation-based publishers; economic incentives; governance controls
Cost Model: Pull-based pricing (protocols pay to update on-chain when needed)
Value at Risk Alignment: High (commonly used in perps and high-frequency DeFi)
Downstream Economic Impact if Incorrect: Severe—can misprice markets, trigger bad liquidations
Centralization Risk: Medium–High (publisher set is permissioned and relatively concentrated)
Known Exploits or Incidents: No major systemic exploit on Ethereum; risks primarily tied to publisher concentration
Description: Market-maker-native oracle network delivering high-frequency price data to Ethereum via a pull-based model
Reason for Inclusion: Publishes authoritative market prices that directly determine protocol economics
Practitioner’s Note: Pyth optimizes for latency and precision; best suited for perps and trading venues, not slow-moving lending markets
Practitioner Validation Check: Verify publisher set, update frequency assumptions, pull costs, and confidence interval handling

On-Chain Footprint: Ethereum mainnet and major L2s via payload-based delivery
Data Source Model: Aggregated off-chain data packaged and delivered on-demand
Verification Mechanism: Off-chain signing + on-chain verification at consumption time
Who Can Submit Data: Permissioned data providers selected per feed
Who Can Challenge Data: Implicit via aggregation; governance-managed provider sets
Freshness Guarantees: On-demand freshness; data delivered when protocol invokes
Availability Guarantees: High—data is available off-chain and delivered with transactions
Failure Handling / Dispute Resolution: Consumer contracts verify signatures; fallback logic handled by protocol
Downstream Economic Impact if Incorrect: Severe—mispricing or logic errors at execution time
Known Exploits or Incidents: No major systemic oracle exploit reported
Description: Modular oracle network that delivers signed price data on-demand instead of continuous on-chain updates
Reason for Inclusion: Publishes authoritative price data consumed directly by smart contracts at execution
Practitioner’s Note: RedStone shifts cost and freshness control to protocols; correctness depends heavily on integration quality
Practitioner Validation Check: Verify integration pattern, signature verification logic, and provider set per feed

Data Source Model: First-party data directly from API providers
Freshness Guarantees: Update cadence defined per API / feed
Downstream Economic Impact if Incorrect: Severe—protocol logic tied directly to API truth
Known Exploits or Incidents: No major Ethereum oracle exploit; adoption still scaling
Description: Oracle network enabling APIs to publish data directly on-chain without intermediaries
Reason for Inclusion: Eliminates oracle middlemen by making data providers the oracle
Practitioner’s Note: First-party model reduces aggregation risk but increases reliance on specific APIs
Practitioner Validation Check: Verify API provider reliability, DAO governance process, and insurance coverage

Freshness Guarantees: Update frequency depends on reporter incentives
Correctness Guarantees: Economic security via staking and slashing
Downstream Economic Impact if Incorrect: High—incorrect data can break protocol logic
Known Exploits or Incidents: Historical disputes resolved via governance; no major systemic exploit
Description: Permissionless oracle allowing anyone to report data secured by staking and disputes
Reason for Inclusion: Provides a censorship-resistant, permissionless oracle alternative
Practitioner’s Note: Strong decentralization, but slower and less predictable updates
Practitioner Validation Check: Verify dispute participation, reporter incentives, and latency tolerance

Verification Mechanism: Optimistic assumption + dispute resolution via token-holder voting
Freshness Guarantees: Event-based; data is final after liveness period
Correctness Guarantees: Correct unless disputed; economic incentives enforce honesty
Failure Handling / Dispute Resolution: Dispute escalation to UMA DAO vote; incorrect proposers slashed
Typical Protocol Dependencies: Synthetic assets, insurance, governance, KPI options
Known Exploits or Incidents: No major unresolved exploit; disputes resolved via governance
Description: Optimistic oracle allowing arbitrary data to be resolved on-chain via economic incentives and disputes
Reason for Inclusion: Enables Ethereum to resolve non-continuous, subjective, or event-based facts
Practitioner’s Note: Best suited for infrequent, high-value assertions; not real-time pricing
Practitioner Validation Check: Validate liveness period, bond sizes, and dispute participation assumptions

Data Source Model: Permissionless reporters fetch and attest to data
Freshness Guarantees: Update cadence depends on request and witness participation
Downstream Economic Impact if Incorrect: High—incorrect data can affect contract outcomes
Known Exploits or Incidents: No major Ethereum oracle exploit reported
Description: Decentralized oracle network using independent witnesses to retrieve and agree on external data
Reason for Inclusion: Provides generalized data attestation with stronger decentralization than API-based models
Practitioner’s Note: Strong decentralization, but slower and less predictable than price oracles
Practitioner Validation Check: Verify witness participation levels and latency tolerance

Primary Data Domain: Subjective facts, governance questions, event outcomes
Who Can Submit Data: Anyone willing to bond an answer
Who Can Challenge Data: Anyone willing to bond a higher-stake answer
Failure Handling / Dispute Resolution: Escalation via bonding; optional arbitration integration
Known Exploits or Incidents: No major systemic exploit; relies on incentive correctness
Description: Oracle system for subjective or human-verifiable facts using economic games
Reason for Inclusion: Allows Ethereum to resolve questions that cannot be objectively computed
Practitioner’s Note: Excellent for governance and human judgment; unsuitable for real-time or high-frequency data
Practitioner Validation Check: Validate arbitration path, bond escalation limits, and user incentives

Primary Data Domain: Cross-chain messages, state, and asset instructions
Data Source Model: Aggregated off-chain reporting from decentralized oracle networks
Verification Mechanism: Decentralized oracle consensus + Risk Management Network (RMN)
Failure Handling / Dispute Resolution: Circuit breakers, RMN halts, governance intervention
Downstream Economic Impact if Incorrect: Catastrophic—incorrect messages can cause asset loss
Known Exploits or Incidents: No major CCIP exploit to date
Description: Cross-chain interoperability protocol enabling secure message and asset transfer between blockchains
Reason for Inclusion: Incorrect messages directly break protocol logic, qualifying CCIP as an oracle
Practitioner’s Note: CCIP prioritizes safety over speed; suitable for high-value, institutional use cases
Practitioner Validation Check: Verify RMN configuration, supported chains, and fee structure

Who Can Submit Data: Permissioned oracle; relayer can be app-selected
Who Can Challenge Data: Applications can choose or replace relayers
Correctness Guarantees: Correctness depends on oracle + relayer independence
Downstream Economic Impact if Incorrect: Catastrophic—message forgery leads to asset loss
Centralization Risk: Medium–High (oracle often centralized; app trust choices)
Known Exploits or Incidents: No Ethereum mainnet exploit; bridge-related risks widely discussed
Description: Messaging protocol enabling applications to send arbitrary messages across chains
Reason for Inclusion: Directly imports cross-chain state; incorrect data breaks protocol logic
Practitioner’s Note: Security depends heavily on oracle–relayer independence chosen by app
Practitioner Validation Check: Validate oracle provider, relayer setup, and default trust assumptions

Known Exploits or Incidents: No major Ethereum exploit; cross-chain risk inherent
Description: Cross-chain network using validator consensus to verify and relay messages
Reason for Inclusion: Validator consensus directly defines cross-chain truth
Practitioner’s Note: Security tied to validator decentralization and stake distribution
Practitioner Validation Check: Verify validator set size, stake distribution, and slashing rules

Description: Cross-chain messaging network relying on guardian attestations
Reason for Inclusion: Incorrect data directly led to large historical losses
Practitioner’s Note: Mature ecosystem but higher trust concentration than newer designs
Practitioner Validation Check: Verify guardian set, quorum rules, and upgrade paths

Primary Data Domain: Arbitrary off-chain computation and API data
On-Chain Footprint: Ethereum mainnet and L2s via Chainlink oracle contracts
Data Source Model: Developer-defined off-chain code calling APIs and services
Verification Mechanism: Decentralized Oracle Network execution + result aggregation
Who Can Challenge Data: Implicit via DON consensus and governance
Failure Handling / Dispute Resolution: Execution retries, DON consensus, governance controls
Downstream Economic Impact if Incorrect: Severe—incorrect computation can mis-set protocol logic
Known Exploits or Incidents: No major exploit reported to date
Description: Serverless compute layer enabling smart contracts to securely call APIs and run off-chain logic
Reason for Inclusion: Imports derived and computed facts on-chain that protocols treat as authoritative
Practitioner’s Note: Powerful but dangerous: correctness depends on developer-written code and API assumptions
Practitioner Validation Check: Audit off-chain code, API trust assumptions, and DON configuration

Data Source Model: Off-chain bots monitor conditions and trigger on-chain execution
Who Can Submit Data: Permissionless executors (with allowlists for some tasks)
Correctness Guarantees: Correctness depends on task logic and execution rules
Downstream Economic Impact if Incorrect: High—bad triggers can mis-execute protocol logic
Known Exploits or Incidents: No major systemic exploit; execution bugs handled per-task
Description: Decentralized automation network that executes and reports on predefined off-chain conditions
Reason for Inclusion: Acts as an oracle when off-chain conditions determine on-chain outcomes
Practitioner’s Note: Often overlooked as an oracle; critical when execution is conditional on off-chain state
Practitioner Validation Check: Verify task definitions, executor set, and failure handling

Correctness Guarantees: Correctness tied to issuer verification process
Downstream Economic Impact if Incorrect: Severe—incorrect attestations can enable fraud or exclusion
Known Exploits or Incidents: No major on-chain exploit; risks are off-chain process related
Description: Identity oracle providing on-chain attestations for KYC, access control, and compliance
Reason for Inclusion: Imports off-chain identity truth directly into smart contracts
Practitioner’s Note: Critical for compliant RWAs; trust shifts from protocol to issuer
Practitioner Validation Check: Validate issuer process, revocation logic, and jurisdictional coverage

Primary Data Domain: Web APIs, TLS-protected data, external facts
Data Source Model: Centralized API calls with cryptographic proofs
Who Can Challenge Data: Not permissionless; limited dispute via verification proofs
Correctness Guarantees: Cryptographic proof of data origin (not economic consensus)
Downstream Economic Impact if Incorrect: High—incorrect data directly affects contract logic
Known Exploits or Incidents: No major exploit; model superseded by newer designs
Description: Early oracle service enabling smart contracts to fetch authenticated web data
Reason for Inclusion: Pioneer of oracle design; still qualifies as authoritative data provider
Practitioner’s Note: Important historically; weaker economic security vs modern oracle networks
Practitioner Validation Check: Verify proof mechanism, current maintenance status, and redundancy

Data Source Model: KPI outcome proposals resolved via optimistic oracle
Who Can Challenge Data: Anyone who disputes via UMA OO
Failure Handling / Dispute Resolution: Dispute escalation to UMA governance vote
Description: KPI Options primitive that settles contracts based on real-world or on-chain performance metrics
Reason for Inclusion: Directly imports off-chain or derived performance truth
Practitioner’s Note: Powerful for incentives and RWAs; not suitable for real-time data
Practitioner Validation Check: Validate KPI definition clarity, bond sizing, and dispute participation

Description: Vertically integrated oracle network offering prices, randomness, and automation
Reason for Inclusion: Publishes authoritative data consumed directly by smart contracts
Practitioner’s Note: Broad feature set increases surface area; practitioners should isolate dependencies
Practitioner Validation Check: Verify validator set size, client diversity, and feature-specific guarantees

Primary Data Domain: Off-chain computation results, network optimization signals
On-Chain Footprint: Ethereum mainnet and L2 integrations (for verification and settlement)
Data Source Model: Off-chain computation performed by network nodes
Verification Mechanism: Cryptographic verification (TEE / zk-style proofs depending on module)
Typical Protocol Dependencies: MEV mitigation, rollups, advanced DeFi infra
Downstream Economic Impact if Incorrect: High—incorrect computation can misroute value or degrade protocol behavior
Centralization Risk: Medium (depends on node and verifier set)
Description: Network providing verifiable off-chain computation and networking services to blockchain protocols
Reason for Inclusion: Qualifies conditionally when computation outputs are treated as authoritative on-chain inputs
Practitioner’s Note: Marlin is not a price oracle; it belongs here only when its computation outputs directly inform on-chain logic
Practitioner Validation Check: Verify which Marlin module is used, proof guarantees, and fallback behavior
